Consider, among other accounts, this anecdote. One day Mîr Dâmâd is late for his class. A merchant has come to the madrasa on important business. Young Mollâ Sadrâ does his duty as host, making conversation to help the visitor wait patiently. Eventually the man asks: “Of this or that molla and Mîr Dâmâd, who is the greater?” Mollâ Sadrâ answers without hesitation: Mîr, his teacher. Just then Mîr Dâmâd arrives at the madrasa, sees the two speaking, and approaches quietly, having thought he heard his name. He hears what follows. The merchant asks: “And between Abû 'Alî Sînâ (Avicenna) and Mîr Dâmâd, who, in your opinion, is the greater?” Once again Mollâ Sadrâ does not hesitate: Mîr. The visitor presses him: “And between the Magister secundus (Mo'allim thâni, that is, al-Fârâbî) and Mîr, who, in your opinion, is the greater?” This time Mollâ Sadrâ hesitates, when a voice suddenly comes from behind him: “Don't be afraid, Sadrâ! Go on, say it: Mîr is the greater!” (Qisas al-'Olamâ, p. 253). ↩

As one example, consider a work published about twenty years ago on “the love of God in non-Christian religions.” It is carefully researched and meticulously thorough in its details. Unfortunately, when the author reaches Safavid Iran, he declares that there is nothing important to report. “The new empire was for a time very powerful [...]. The arts flourished. But there were no mystical writers or Sufis of distinction. The same holds for the Qajar period, which began in 1794.” (“... ist hier nichts wichtiges zu berichten. Das neue Reich war zeitweise sehr mächtig [...]. Die Künste blühten. Aber mystische Schriftsteller und Sûfî von Rang gab es nicht. An Iranologist can only read such statements in astonishment! How could an entire spiritual culture have remained so inaccessible to Western theological scholarship? Another important recent work by the same shaykh is Shî'a dar Islam (Shiism in Islam, Tehran, 1348/1969). Among works published for the four-hundredth anniversary of Mollâ Sadrâ's birth, we should particularly mention his Persian treatise Seh Asl (The Three Sources), together with his mathnawî and rubâ'îyât, edited with introduction and notes by Seyyed Hosseïn Nasr (Faculty of Theology, Tehran University), 1380 lunar Hijri/1961. By Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî: Sharh-e hâl o ârâ-ye falsafa-ye Mollâ Sadrâ (biography and philosophical doctrines of Mollâ Sadrâ), Mashhad, 1341 solar Hijri; Hastî, az nazar-e falsafa o 'irfân (Being, from the Perspectives of Philosophy and Mysticism), Mashhad, 1380 lunar Hijri; his editions of Mazâhir al-ilâhîya, Mashhad, 1380 lunar Hijri, and Shawâhid al-robûbîya, Mashhad, 1968; and the Anthologie announced above, p. 12, n. 6. By M.-T. Dânesh-Pajûh: the edition of Kasr asnâm al-jâhilîya (The Shattering of the Idols of Ignorance, directed against a certain kind of Sufism), Tehran, 1340 solar Hijri/1961. Of our own work: our edition and translation of Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques (Kitâb al-mashâ'ir) (Bibl. Ir., vol. 10), Tehran–Paris, 1964. S. J. Ashtiyânî also edited Moh. Ja'far Langarûdî's commentary on this work by Mollâ Sadrâ, Mashhad, 1964. We should recall our two studies: La Place de Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî dans la philosophie iranienne, in Studia Islamica, fasc. XVIII, Paris, 1962, pp. 81–113; and Le Thème de la résurrection chez Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, commentateur de Sohrawardî, in Studies in Mysticism and Religion Presented to Gershom G. Scholem on His Seventieth Birthday, Jerusalem, 1967, pp. 71–116. The main substance of these two studies is incorporated here. In addition, at the École des Hautes-Études we devoted three years of lectures to the major work that most fully expresses Mollâ Sadrâ as a Shiite philosopher: his commentary on Kolaynî's Osûl mina'l-Kâfi. See the summaries in the Annuaire de la Section des Sciences religieuses of the École pratique des Hautes Études, 1962–1963, pp. 69 ff.; 1963–1964, pp. 73 ff.; 1964–1965, pp. 85 ff. Finally, see the passages from Mollâ Sadrâ translated in our Terre céleste et corps de résurrection..., pp. 257–265. They come from the “Book of the Theosophy of the Throne” (Hikmat 'arshîya) and concern spissitudo spiritualis (spiritual density); see also Chapter IV of our French introduction to Anthologie I. ↩
M. Meshkâtoddînî's recent book Nazarîbe-falsafa-ye Sadroddîn-e Shîrâzî (Tehran, 1966), despite the best of intentions, perhaps yields rather too much to this temptation. ↩

See above, n. 6. “Tradition” is not a funeral procession; if it is not to look like one, it must be a perpetual rebirth. Indeed, there can be no initiation into traditional philosophy without a new spiritual birth. This is surely something the young Iranians who are taking an interest in that revival today are experiencing. ↩

Allâhwêrdî Khân, succeeded by his son Imâm Qolî-Khân, governed Fârs from AH 1003 and died in AH 1021. See M.-T. Dânesh-Pajûh's introduction to his edition of Kasr asnâm... (above, p. 55, n. 75), pp. 2 ff. We might suppose that Mollâ Sadrâ returned to Shiraz between AH 1003 and 1010; his teaching there would then have extended over some forty years. The difficulty is that the madrasa was not completed until 1022/1613, a year after Allâhwêrdî Khân's death (see the frontispiece photograph in our edition and translation of Mashâ'ir). Mollâ Sadrâ could, however, have begun teaching before its completion. On the other hand, using dates from the biography of Mohsen Fayz, Mollâ Sadrâ's pupil and son-in-law, cited by Sayyed Mohammad Meshkât in his preface to volume IV of his edition of Kitâb al-Mahajjat al-bayzâ (Tehran, 1339 solar Hijri), M. Dânesh-Pajûh proposes moving Mollâ Sadrâ's return to Shiraz as late as AH 1042. That date seems far too late. The truth doubtless lies somewhere between the two extremes; no more can be said here. See our introduction to Mashâ'ir, p. 8 and p. 23, nn. 12–13. ↩

Three typeset editions of Kolaynî's great work have recently appeared in Tehran through the efforts of Shaykh Akhûndî: first, an eight-volume edition of the Arabic text alone, Tehran, 1334 solar Hijri/1955; then an edition of the Arabic Osûl, with a Persian translation and commentary by Shaykh Moh. Bâqir Kamra'î, Tehran, 1961 onward; and finally an edition of the Osûl with the commentary of Moh. Sâlih Mazandarânî (d. ca. 1081–1086/1670–1676), Tehran, 1382 lunar Hijri/1963 onward, of which twelve volumes have appeared. ↩

Mollâ Sadrâ had time to comment on the Kitâb al-'Aql (Book of the Intellect) and the Kitâb al-Tawhîd, and to begin commenting on the Kitâb al-Hojjat (which contains the Imams' teachings on prophecy and the Imamate). Although he could comment on only about a tenth of this book, so crucial to Shiite thought, the lithographic edition of his commentary (Tehran, undated)—a profoundly original work—still runs to 450 folio pages. See our reports in the Annuaire de la Section des Sciences religieuses, cited above at p. 55, n. 75, and our introduction to Mashâ'ir, p. 38, bibliography no. 33. ↩

His commentaries were brought together in the lithographic edition of his Tafsîr, Shiraz, AH 1322 (approximately 700 folio pages). Two other works are inseparable from them: Mafâtih al-ghayb (Keys to the Unseen World), printed lithographically after the commentary on the Osûl mina'l-Kâfî, and Asrâr al-Âyât (The Esoteric Meanings of the Verses, or “Signs”). We shall return to them elsewhere. See bibliography nos. 4, 21, and 35. ↩

See above, p. 55, n. 75, and our introduction to Mashâ'ir, bibliography no. 10, pp. 30–32, listing the numerous commentaries prompted by this vast work, whose author was a true intellectual master. On the very idea of these “four journeys,” see the discussion below. ↩

Let us mention that there are at least half a dozen commentaries each on Mashâ'ir and Hikmat 'arshîya (bibliography nos. 9 and 22). Hâdî Sabzavârî wrote complete commentaries on the Asfâr and Shawâhid al-robûbiya. See also M.-T. Dânesh-Pajûh, op. cit., introduction, pp. 23 ff. We should remember that journals and periodicals did not yet exist: research advanced and deepened through these commentaries. None of them, therefore, can be dismissed as unimportant. ↩
